proposals.name: Compression: implication per word
proposals.instruction: Score how much inferential work the caption sets in motion relative to how many words it spends. A 10 is a caption of roughly one to six words that nonetheless commits the reader to a whole situation, relationship, or reframing -- every word is load-bearing and nothing can be deleted without destroying it. A 5 is a caption of ordinary sentence length whose content matches its length. A 0 is a caption that spends many words to deliver a single small idea, where a reader could cut half the words and lose nothing. Judge word-economy against payload only; do not reward shortness by itself if the short line carries no implication.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side of the slice is dominated by extreme compression: R22 ('you're rambling again', 3 words), R26 ('it's so ewe'), R51 ('he got indicted'), R54 ('wreckmaninoff', one word), R20 ('republican primary ticket'). The card-high side runs long and loose: R33, R45, R41, R29. A bank built from written criteria will tend to reward legible, complete, well-formed sentences and will read a three-word line as thin; the dense model appears to be pricing density, not length.

proposals.name: Cold open with no conversational preamble
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption begins directly on its content. A 10 starts mid-stance with no runway: no greeting, no hedge, no discourse marker, no throat-clearing. A 0 opens with padding that carries no joke -- e.g. 'i don't know about you, but', 'believe it or not', 'okay, okay, fine', 'actually', 'guess i'll go ahead and', 'hope you don't mind', 'are you sure' -- or otherwise spends its first clause getting ready to speak. Score the opening only; ignore how good the eventual content is.
proposals.rationale: Nearly every card-high row opens with a softener: R06 ('i don't know about you, but'), R32 ('believe it or not'), R49 ('okay, okay. fine'), R40 ('guess i'll go ahead and'), R50 ('actually'), R02 ('hope you don't mind'), R41 ('are you sure'). Dense-high rows open cold: R04, R51, R58, R22. Preamble makes a line read as fluent and polite -- exactly the surface a criterion bank scores well -- while adding zero comic content.

proposals.name: Requires the drawing to complete it
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption depends on an unseen image to become meaningful. A 10 is nearly inert on the page -- a flat, ordinary line whose only possible interest is the collision between its plainness and whatever is depicted; read alone it looks almost empty. A 0 is fully self-contained: the caption carries its whole joke in the text and a drawing would add nothing. Score dependence, not quality; a judge reading text alone should mark a caption HIGH here precisely when the text alone leaves them unable to see the joke but able to see that a specific, strange picture would supply it.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('you're rambling again'), R35 ('you need to get your act together'), R21 ('i love that it's 100 wool') and R04 ('i don't tell you how to gather') are near-empty as text yet sit at dense_pct .99/.99/.95/.98. A text-only scorecard has no way to credit a line whose entire function is to be completed by a picture, so it scores them low (card .395/.412/.276/.386). This is likely the single largest source of the dense-high/card-low direction.

proposals.name: Does not narrate its own joke
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption trusts the reader. A 10 states the funny thing and stops -- no evaluation of it, no signposting, no reaction word. A 0 tells the reader that a joke has occurred or how to feel about it: appending an assessment ('it's hysterical'), flagging that a pattern exists ('i think there's a theme'), or otherwise supplying the reaction the reader should have had. Mid scores for lines that only mildly nudge. Judge only the presence of self-commentary.
proposals.rationale: R11 ends with 'it's hysterical', which does the laughing for the reader, and R57 announces 'i think there's a theme'; both are card-high (.762, .890) and dense-low (.142, .128). R30 similarly explains its own premise. A criterion bank tends to credit clarity and explicitness; self-narration reads as clear while destroying the comic mechanism.

proposals.name: Buried load-bearing wordplay, not framed and delivered
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score wordplay on two things together: (a) whether the pun carries the whole caption rather than sitting inside a larger explanatory sentence, and (b) whether it is left unframed for the reader to catch. A 10 is a pun deployed with no scaffolding, in a sentence that would be perfectly ordinary if you did not hear the second meaning. A 0 is a pun that arrives inside a frame announcing that a pun is coming -- a correction frame, a 'you'll love it' recommendation, a long setup clause -- or a pun that is explained after being made. Score 0 also for no wordplay at all only if the caption's apparent bid was wordplay and it failed to land one.
proposals.rationale: Unframed, load-bearing puns are dense-high: R39 ('i suspect vowel play'), R26 ('it's so ewe'), R54 ('wreckmaninoff'), R08 ('cross word'), R58/R60 ('no quarter'). Framed and delivered puns are card-high: R03 ('no, that's a blues jay' -- correction frame), R29 ('hole-in-the-wall place you'll love' -- recommendation frame), R33 ('he's doing a cover' -- long expository setup). The bank appears to credit legible wordplay regardless of staging; the dense model prices the staging.

proposals.name: Transgressive content delivered deadpan
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score the product of nerve and flatness of delivery. A 10 says something risky -- crude, dark, morbid, sexual, or socially forbidden -- in a completely level, unexcited register, with no wink, no exclamation point, and no apology. A 5 is either safe-but-deadpan or edgy-but-loudly-signalled. A 0 is safe content delivered with performed comic energy. Do not score the content's offensiveness as a defect here; score whether the caption takes a real risk and whether it holds a straight face while doing it.
proposals.rationale: The most extreme card-low rows are the riskiest: R12 ('exposed skin implies consent', card .017), R10 ('you should see the breasts', card .038), R19 ('my dad lost a leg', card .085), R36 ('pooped', card .047), R55 ('still want to see my bedroom'). All are dense-high (.859/.929/.656/.741/.917). A written criterion bank almost certainly contains taste, decency, or inoffensiveness language that actively penalizes exactly the risk-taking the dense model rewards.

proposals.name: Live, specific real-world anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption plants itself in a specific, nameable piece of the real world -- a political faction, an institution, a named person, a named work -- as opposed to a generic situation or an exhausted mass-culture catchphrase. A 10 names or unmistakably invokes something specific and currently contested. A 5 references something real but broad. A 0 either references nothing outside the frame or leans on a catchphrase so worn that it functions as filler rather than reference. Score specificity and liveness of the reference, not whether you personally find the reference agreeable.
proposals.rationale: A whole cluster of political-anchor rows is dense-high and card-near-zero: R15 ('republican slate', card .028), R20 ('republican primary ticket', .042), R05 ('white house collection', .325), R28 ('still looking for votes', .093), R51 ('he got indicted', .348). The contrast case is R16 ('six feet dude. six. feet'), a stale pandemic catchphrase that is card-high (.977) and dense-lowest-decile (.040). The bank seems to reward topical-sounding surface without distinguishing live specificity from exhausted meme.

proposals.name: Not the maximally available first thought
proposals.instruction: Score how far the caption is from the line most people would produce first. A 10 is a construction you would not have predicted from the situation -- an angle that had to be found. A 0 is a recycled frame filled in: 'what i'd really like to do is direct', 'does this make my X look big', 'it's not an X problem, it's a Y problem', 'life is short, eat dessert first', 'what are we, animals?'. Judge the template, not the topic: a caption can be locally well-written and still score 0 here because its skeleton is off the shelf.
proposals.rationale: The card-high side is thick with stock skeletons: R17 (the 'really want to direct' template), R13 and R25 (both the 'does this make me look big' template), R24 and R40 (both the 'eat dessert first' cliche), R09 ('it's not an X problem it's a Y problem'), R53 ('what are we, neanderthals'). The near-duplicate pairs R13/R25 and R24/R40 are direct evidence that these are default reachings. Template lines are grammatical, punchy-shaped and easy to score well on written craft criteria, which is likely why the card overrates them.

proposals.name: Oddly specific detail implying an offstage world
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption drops a concrete, unexplained particular -- a number, a time, a count, a measurement -- that implies a whole history or institution outside the frame that the reader must reconstruct. A 10 supplies a precise, strange, unexplained figure that only makes sense if a large unseen backstory exists. A 5 has some concreteness but nothing that opens onto an unseen world. A 0 is entirely generic, with no particulars, or supplies numbers that are merely descriptive of what is present.
proposals.rationale: R59 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up', dense .741 / card .091), R18 ('given we had 500 this morning', .880/.115), R14 ('soccer practice at 2 30', .640/.085) and R34 ('88 keys and no locks', .714/.089) all invoke an unexplained offstage regime. All four are strongly card-low. A text-only bank likely reads an unexplained number as unclear or confusing rather than as world-building.

proposals.name: Avoids restating what is already visible
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the caption is spent describing the scene rather than adding to it. A 10 adds information or a stance that no viewer could have gotten by looking. A 0 is pure narration of the obvious -- confirming an object's location, naming its material, confirming who the speakers are, or enumerating the visible cast. Mid scores for captions that restate one visible fact in service of a real turn. Judge only the redundancy, treating the caption's own nouns as evidence of what is depicted.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('the remote is in your hand'), R52 ('the remote is plastic, right'), R37 ('yes we are your upstairs neighbors- how did you know'), R50 (an enumerated list of pets) and R32 ('they think that we look alike too') are all card-high (.794/.864/.679/.938/.767) and dense-low (.225/.313/.163/.415/.087). These captions are informative and coherent as standalone text, which a text-only bank rewards, while contributing nothing the picture did not already say.

proposals.name: Borrowed institutional register used with precision
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption speaks in a recognizable specialist or genre idiom -- martial, legal, clinical, bureaucratic, HR, therapeutic, debate-panel -- and whether it gets that idiom exactly right. A 10 sustains a borrowed register accurately for the whole line, so that the register itself is the joke's vehicle. A 5 gestures at a register with generic vocabulary. A 0 is undifferentiated everyday speech with no register to speak of. Score fidelity to the borrowed idiom, not the subject matter.
proposals.rationale: R58 and R60 ('no quarter will be given') hold a martial idiom; R12 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent') holds panel-debate diction exactly; R43 ('a two-step program') holds recovery-speak; R46 ('all my evaluation said was good girl') holds performance-review diction; R47 holds a clinical euphemism. Every one is dense-high and card-low (e.g. R58 .945/.268, R12 .859/.017). Register fidelity is hard to capture in a written criterion, so the bank misses it entirely.

proposals.name: Implies an ongoing relationship and prior grievance
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line reads as one turn inside a long-running relationship rather than a first exchange. A 10 presupposes shared history -- an argument already had many times, a standing division of labor, a repeated complaint -- signalled by words like 'again', 'until now', 'still', or by a rebuke that only makes sense between intimates. A 0 is an opening line between strangers, or an utterance with no implied prior turn at all. Score only the implied history, not whether the relationship is pleasant.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('i don't tell you how to gather') presupposes an entire settled domestic economy; R22 ('you're rambling again') and R35 ('get your act together') presuppose a repeated complaint; R08 ('until now... we have never had a cross word between us') and R59 ('and then you show up') presuppose long shared history. All are dense-high with card .386/.395/.412/.134/.091. Presupposed history is invisible to criteria that score what the text asserts.

proposals.name: Startling implied identity for the speaker
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption quietly reveals that whoever is speaking is not who the reader assumed. A 10 makes the speaker's identity itself the surprise -- the line is unremarkable until you work out who must be saying it, at which point the whole caption reorganizes. A 5 has a mildly unexpected speaker. A 0 is spoken by exactly the person you would expect, or gives no identity information at all. Score the identity reveal, not the wit of the wording.
proposals.rationale: R46 ('all my evaluation said was good girl') reorganizes once you place the speaker; R21 ('i love that it's 100 wool') and R26 ('it's so ewe') hinge entirely on who is speaking; R04 does the same. All four sit at dense .827/.949/.981/.976 with card .121/.276/.153/.386. Compare card-high R37 and R32, where the speakers are exactly who they appear to be. A text-only bank scores the sentence, not the inference about its speaker.

proposals.name: No expository setup clause doing the drawing's work
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption is built as a single utterance or as an explicit setup-then-punchline pair. A 10 is one undivided utterance; the reader gets no scaffolding. A 0 devotes a leading clause or sentence to establishing context the picture already establishes -- a professional self-description before the twist, a stated premise before the reversal, a question asked only so it can be answered. Mid scores for captions with a short pivot that still carries content. Score structure only.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but...') spends a full clause explaining the speaker's competence before turning; R41, R30, R29 and R06 all build the same two-part scaffold. Each is card-high (.913/.590/.713/.771/.924) and among the lowest dense rows in the slice (.006/.028/.097/.170/.155). Two-part structure is the textbook shape of a written joke, so a bank scoring joke-craft rewards it, but in a captioned cartoon the setup is redundant with the image.

proposals.name: Payload lands last, with no trailing softener
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score (a) whether the caption's heaviest word or idea sits at the very end and (b) whether anything follows it. A 10 ends on the payload and stops dead. A 0 places the payload early and then trails off -- appending a tag question ('right?', 'why', 'how did you know'), a politeness coda ('that would be great'), an evaluation, or drifting punctuation. Mid scores for captions that land late but add one small word after. Judge placement and terminal cleanliness only.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high rows end on their heaviest beat and stop: R59 ('...and then you show up'), R14 ('soccer practice at 2 30'), R19 ('...and my dad lost a leg'), R58 ('no quarter will be given'). Card-high and weak-dense rows trail: R52 ends '...right', R42 ends 'why', R37 ends 'how did you know', R45 ends 'that would be great', and R31 trails into '.... --' while sitting at card .034. Terminal rhythm is a performance property that written criteria rarely encode.

proposals.name: Verbal bulk: word count and clause count
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the sheer verbal bulk of the caption, counted mechanically. 0 = a single word or a bare noun phrase of three words or fewer with no finite verb; 3 = one short clause of roughly four to seven words; 6 = one complete sentence of roughly eight to twelve words; 8 = thirteen to sixteen words or two independent clauses; 10 = seventeen or more words, or two or more separate sentences, or a sentence plus a trailing follow-up. Count words and clauses and read the number off this scale. You must NOT judge whether the length suits the caption, whether the caption is funny, whether it is economical, or whether it is good in any way. A one-word caption and a twenty-word caption can both be excellent; you are scoring only how much text there is.
proposals.rationale: Length is almost perfectly confounded with the disagreement axis in this slice and has nothing to do with contest merit. The shortest items sit on the dense_high_card_low side -- R07 is a single word ('wreckmaninoff', dense_pct 0.794 vs card_pct 0.140), R23 is three words ('he got indicted', 0.957 vs 0.348), R40 is three words (0.751 vs 0.042), R58 is four words (0.981 vs 0.153). The longest items sit on the dense_low_card_high side -- R45 is seventeen words (0.006 vs 0.913), R35 is sixteen words (0.028 vs 0.590), R02 is thirteen words (0.259 vs 0.824), R24 is fourteen words (0.170 vs 0.771). A criterion bank scored 0-10 per criterion mechanically rewards items that give each criterion something to grade, so verbosity buys card_pct; the dense model does not pay it. Either way, word count is not a property of how good a caption is.

proposals.name: Conversational hedge and discourse-marker scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the caption is occupied by pre-punch conversational scaffolding: sentence-initial hedges and discourse markers ('guess I'll', 'I don't know about you, but', 'believe it or not', 'okay, okay, fine', 'actually', 'in that case', 'hope you don't mind', 'enough about me', 'yes, we all', 'you know ..., right'), politeness softeners, concessives, and filler that precedes the substantive content. 0 = the caption opens directly on its content with no such material; 5 = one clear marker or softener occupying a small fraction of the line; 10 = the caption opens with scaffolding and contains two or more such markers, so that a substantial share of the words are framing rather than content. Score the extent of the scaffolding only. You must NOT judge whether the scaffolding makes the line sound natural, well-voiced, or funny -- naturalism is often a virtue here, and that is exactly what you are being told to ignore.
proposals.rationale: Hedge scaffolding is one-sided in this slice and is a stylistic habit, not a merit. R01 opens 'guess i'll go ahead and' (dense 0.242 / card 0.822), R02 opens 'hope you don't mind' (0.259 / 0.824), R26 opens 'i don't know about you, but' (0.155 / 0.924), R43 opens 'okay, okay. fine' (0.313 / 0.849), R51 opens 'believe it or not' (0.087 / 0.811), R60 opens 'actually' (0.415 / 0.938). All six are dense_low_card_high. A criterion bank containing anything like 'reads as natural speech' or 'establishes a speaker voice' will be systematically fed by this filler while the dense model discounts it, so it predicts card_pct without being contest quality.

proposals.name: Orthographic or phonetic manipulation of a name or fixed phrase
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible letter-level or sound-level manipulation performed on a proper name, title, or fixed phrase: portmanteaus, homophone respellings, one-letter substitutions, and phrase blends. 0 = every word appears in its ordinary form and no fixed phrase has been altered; 3 = a fixed phrase is quoted intact with no alteration; 6 = one word is swapped for a near-homophone inside an otherwise standard phrase; 10 = a proper name or fixed phrase has been visibly rewritten at the letter level, or the whole caption is such a coinage. Judge only how much orthographic or phonetic surgery is visible in the string. You must NOT judge whether the wordplay lands, whether it is clever, groan-worthy, or apt to any picture. Score the mechanism, not the effect.
proposals.rationale: Pun mechanics are a stylistic signature of a subpopulation of submitters rather than a quality dimension, and they split the two models sharply. R07 is a pure coinage ('wreckmaninoff', dense 0.794 / card 0.140), R58 substitutes one homophone ('it's so ewe', 0.981 / 0.153), R37 blends a fixed phrase ('i suspect vowel play' from 'foul play', 0.867 / 0.306), and R31 does the same in the opposite direction ('no, that's a blues jay', 0.148 / 0.679). A criterion bank scoring things like clarity, situational fit, or speaker plausibility cannot see the mechanism at all and marks these near the floor, while the dense model rewards them. Tagged mixed because a submitter with real pun-writing practice may also write genuinely better contest entries.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's habitual wordplay practice / puzzle-and-pun writing background

proposals.name: Numeric and quantitative specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much explicit quantity the caption contains: digits, spelled-out numbers, counts, measurements, durations, times of day, percentages, and prices. 0 = no numeric content of any kind; 3 = one vague quantifier only ('a few', 'plenty'); 6 = one explicit number; 8 = one explicit number carrying a unit or a period of time; 10 = two or more explicit numbers, or a number given unusual emphasis by repetition or punctuation. Count what is on the page. You must NOT judge whether the number is well chosen, whether specificity improves the line, or whether the caption is funny. Precise numbers are often a comic virtue; you are being asked to ignore that and report only the extent of numeric content.
proposals.rationale: Explicit quantities cluster on the dense_high_card_low side while the scorecard treats them as unscorable noise. R57 ('581 days without an accident', dense 0.741 / card 0.091), R56 ('we had 500 this morning', 0.880 / 0.115), R20 ('the house has 88 keys', 0.714 / 0.089), R04 ('lost 45 pounds', 0.656 / 0.095), R55 ('it's 100 wool', 0.949 / 0.276) and R29 ('soccer practice at 2 30', 0.640 / 0.085) are all high-dense, low-card. The count of digits in a string is not a property of how good the entry is. Note a partial confound with B08: some of these numbers ('88 keys', '100 wool') are picture-anchored, so the two channels should be read together rather than summed.

proposals.name: Venue house-register: professional-class urban domestic vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the caption's vocabulary and implied situation sit inside a particular social register: salaried professional, urban or suburban, domestic and small-talk life -- spouses and in-laws, apartment neighbours and building rules, office reviews and job titles, restaurants and takeout and grocery provenance, pets, paperwork. 0 = nothing in the wording places the speaker in that world; 5 = one lexical item or situation from that world; 10 = the vocabulary, the situation and the manners are all drawn from it, with two or more such markers. Score only how strongly the register is signalled by the words present. You must NOT judge whether that register is appropriate, tasteful, well-observed, or well-matched to anything. You are measuring a dialect, not its merit.
proposals.rationale: Long-running caption contests train their regulars in a recognisable house voice, and that voice leaves a lexical trace even when the joke underneath is weak. Every strong instance here is dense_low_card_high: R03 'you're sure it's wild caught? my in-laws can tell' (0.036 / 0.631), R49 'you're an accountant? that must be exciting' (0.065 / 0.811), R24 'if you're free after work, i know this hole-in-the-wall place' (0.170 / 0.771), R42 'yes we are your upstairs neighbors' (0.163 / 0.679), R60 'no dogs, cats or other small pets' (0.415 / 0.938). The fingerprint is the register lexicon, which a judge can see; the upstream factor (how many past winners the author has absorbed) is unobservable and must not be scored. Tagged mixed because the same enculturation plausibly also teaches genuine craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: author enculturation in the venue's house style (repeat contestants who have read hundreds of published winners)

proposals.name: Electoral and news-cycle political referents
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption refers to electoral politics, government institutions, or legal-political events: parties, primaries, slates, tickets, ballots, votes, indictments, offices of government, named political figures. 0 = no political or governmental referent; 3 = a word with a faint political shading used non-politically; 6 = one clear political referent; 10 = the caption is built entirely around a political or electoral referent and would be unintelligible without it. Report only how much such reference is present. You must NOT judge whether the political material is timely, pointed, tired, funny, partisan, or well used, and you must not favour or disfavour any political position.
proposals.rationale: The unseen factor is when the caption was written -- a contest running during a primary season or an indictment week fills with politics regardless of caption merit. The fingerprint is the political vocabulary itself, and it is perfectly one-sided in this slice: R23 'he got indicted' (0.957 / 0.348), R27 'they're still looking for votes' (0.970 / 0.093), R40 'republican primary ticket' (0.751 / 0.042), R54 'it's the republican slate of candidates' (0.764 / 0.028), R39 'from our new white house collection' (0.940 / 0.325). A criterion bank scoring self-containedness or situational clarity floors these; the dense model, which has absorbed the era's news-inflected corpus, ranks them at the top. Calendar position is not caption quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to the news cycle at the moment of the contest round

proposals.name: Era-dating situational idiom and euphemism
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption relies on a situational idiom that dates it to a particular period: physical-distancing language, delivery and takeout as a default, coy euphemism for a shared ongoing situation ('the you know what'), household paperwork drives such as a census. 0 = the situation described could belong to any decade; 5 = one dating idiom present but incidental; 10 = the caption's whole premise is a period-specific situation and it would read as a non-sequitur outside that period. Report only how strongly the wording dates the caption. You must NOT judge whether the period reference is fresh, stale, over-used, or funny -- topicality is neither a credit nor a penalty here.
proposals.rationale: This is the same upstream factor as B06 -- submission date -- but with a different fingerprint and, importantly, the opposite sign in this slice, which is why it must be a separate channel. R32 'six feet dude. six. feet' (dense 0.040 / card 0.977), R26 'i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout' (0.155 / 0.924), R33 'we can't talk about the you know what' (0.276 / 0.883) and R43 'fine, i'll fill out the census' (0.313 / 0.849) are all dense_low_card_high, whereas the political-referent items in B06 are all dense_high_card_low. Merging the two would produce a non-monotone channel. When the caption was written is not how good it is.
proposals.upstream_parent: the calendar date of the contest round (corpus vintage)

proposals.name: Picture-anchored concrete nouns from a single drawing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the caption's content words name concrete objects, animals, materials or actions that a writer could only have produced while looking at one specific drawing -- e.g. a named animal or breed, a fibre or material, a specific piece of household hardware, a specific animal-handling verb or command. 0 = every content word is generic conversational vocabulary that could accompany any picture; 5 = one such picture-anchored noun or verb; 10 = two or more, so that the caption is lexically welded to one image. Report only how picture-specific the vocabulary is. You must NOT judge whether the anchoring is apt, whether it explains or over-explains the drawing, or whether the caption is funny; both heavily anchored and wholly generic captions can be excellent.
proposals.rationale: Round identity is invisible to a text-only model but leaves a hard lexical trace, and different rounds attract different crowd sizes and different competition levels, so round membership predicts an item's fate independently of the item. The wool/sheep round shows up as R13 'pull the wool over my eyes' (0.876 / 0.170), R55 'i love that it's 100 wool' (0.949 / 0.276) and R58 'it's so ewe' (0.981 / 0.153) -- all dense_high_card_low. The bear/salmon round shows up as R10 'no bag. in fact, if you could toss it at me' (0.043 / 0.641) and R17 'no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon' (0.338 / 0.991) -- both dense_low_card_high. The dog-training round appears as R05 'herding is okay' (0.094 / 0.769) and R52 'when you've mastered sit and stay' (0.208 / 0.794). Scoring the fingerprint is fair; scoring the round is not, and the judge cannot see the round anyway.
proposals.upstream_parent: which cartoon the caption was submitted to (round identity, round crowd size and round difficulty)

proposals.name: Transgressive bodily, sexual, or injury content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of norm-testing content: sexual reference or innuendo, nudity or exposure, anatomy, scatological or bathroom reference, bodily injury, dismemberment, death, addiction, or consent as a topic. 0 = nothing a general-audience publication would pause over; 3 = a mild double meaning available only on a second reading; 6 = one clear reference of this kind; 10 = the caption's central content is explicitly of this kind. Report only how much such content is present. You must NOT judge whether it is gratuitous, brave, tasteless, or funny, and you must not apply your own tolerance threshold as a quality signal; edgy captions and clean captions can be equally good.
proposals.rationale: A publication's screening norms are an unseen process factor that shapes which registers thrive, and the fingerprint -- transgressive content words -- is fully visible. In this slice it is one-sided: R18 'exposed skin implies consent' (0.859 / 0.017), R36 'you should see the breasts' (0.929 / 0.038), R19 'we'll be pooped by the end of the night' (0.741 / 0.047), R50 'still want to see my bedroom' (0.917 / 0.335), R04 'my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg' (0.656 / 0.095), R44 'entering a two-step program' (0.802 / 0.216). A criterion bank almost certainly encodes decorum somewhere and floors all of them; the dense model, trained on unfiltered comic text, ranks them high. Tagged mixed because willingness to take a risk plausibly correlates with genuinely stronger comic writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: editorial gatekeeping norms on the receiving side, and the corresponding self-censorship pressure on submitters

proposals.name: High-collision stock template framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the caption occupies a stock, template-shaped slot that many independent writers would be likely to land on: a fixed comic frame ('I'll have my X first'), a stock question form ('does this make my X look Y'), a stock domestic complaint, a stock refusal, or a widely known set phrase used with no alteration. Ask yourself: if a hundred people wrote a line for this situation, how many would produce something near-identical in wording and structure? 0 = an idiosyncratic construction you would expect from at most one writer; 5 = a recognisable frame with individual wording; 10 = a template so common that near-duplicates are almost guaranteed. Report only the collision likelihood of the framing. You must NOT judge whether the template is hackneyed, obvious, elegant, or funny -- a widely shared framing can be the best entry in a contest, and you are not scoring that.
proposals.rationale: Near-duplicate pairs are visible inside this 60-row slice, which is direct evidence that template collision is a live upstream factor and that it moves the two models differently. R01 'guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first' (0.242 / 0.822) and R08 'in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first' (0.338 / 0.824) are the same joke slot; so are R21 'do you think it makes my teeth look big' (0.214 / 0.955) and R47 'do my teeth look big in this' (0.474 / 0.979); so are R16 'no. no quarter will be given' (0.945 / 0.268) and R25 'i will give you no quarter' (0.994 / 0.355); so are R28 'you know the remote is plastic, right' (0.313 / 0.864) and R53 'honey, the remote is in your hand' (0.225 / 0.794). A criterion bank rewards the legibility of a familiar frame while the dense model discounts what it has seen a thousand times. Tagged mixed because a framing the drawing naturally invites may also be genuinely the right read of the picture.
proposals.upstream_parent: crowd dynamics of mass simultaneous submission (duplicate and near-duplicate convergence within a round)

proposals.name: Idiom literalized into the depicted scene
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption takes a familiar idiom or fixed expression and deploys it so it reads simultaneously as literally true of the pictured scene and as the idiom's ordinary figurative meaning, with the double reading compressed into very few words. Score 0 if the caption contains no idiom/fixed-expression play, or if a literal reading and a figurative reading do not both resolve.
proposals.rationale: R01 'no. no quarter will be given' and R14 'i will give you no quarter' both re-stage the pirate-mercy idiom literally; R13 'could you pull the wool over my eyes' and R22 'it's so ewe' do the same with sheep idioms. All four are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Payload compressed into the terminal word
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption is inert or unremarkable until its very last word or short final phrase, at which point a single word supplies the entire comic turn. Score 0 if the payoff is spread across the sentence, arrives mid-sentence, or there is no distinct final-word turn.
proposals.rationale: R22 'it's so ewe' and R33 'i suspect vowel play' both hinge entirely on their last word/phrase; R53 'it's from our new white house collection' saves its reveal for the final two words. All three are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Clash of incongruous registers in one line
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption yokes two clearly mismatched registers (e.g., epic/historical/violent/legalistic language set directly against mundane domestic content) inside a single short line. Score 0 if the caption maintains one consistent, unremarkable register throughout.
proposals.rationale: R05 'you can't invade russia today. soccer practice at 2 30' collides historical-military language with a scheduling note; R06 'where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent' collides clinical/legalistic phrasing with a charged topic. Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Dark or taboo content delivered flatly
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption references injury, death, crime, or otherwise taboo material and states it in a flat, unemotional, matter-of-fact tone with no softening. Score 0 if the caption is wholly anodyne and family-safe, or if dark content is present but delivered with visible emotional flourish rather than deadpan understatement.
proposals.rationale: R31 'my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg' and R60 '581 days without an accident, and then you show up' both state grim facts in a flat register; R21 'he got indicted' does the same for a legal/political blow. All three dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Single line implies a larger untold history
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the one-line caption unmistakably gestures at a specific, larger sequence of prior events (a running pattern, a history, a prior incident) that the reader must reconstruct beyond the pictured instant. Score 0 if the caption is fully self-contained, describing only the pictured moment with no implied backstory.
proposals.rationale: R24 'you're very calm, given we had 500 this morning' and R60 '581 days without an accident, and then you show up' both compress an implied running history into a single number; R55 'we can say we saw him before he took off' implies a prior conspiratorial event. All dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Payoff depends on a specific outside reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption's humor requires the reader to recognize and map on a specific external reference -- a named person/work (composer, detective story), a folk song, or a live topical/political situation -- onto the pictured scene. Score 0 if the caption requires no outside cultural or topical knowledge whatsoever.
proposals.rationale: R19 'my dear watson, we have never had a cross word between us' needs the Holmes/crossword mapping and R08 'wreckmaninoff' needs the Rachmaninoff mapping; R25/R27/R49/R21/R53 all lean on live political material (primary ticket, slate of candidates, votes, indicted, white house). All dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Freshness relative to stock contest punchlines
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption reuses a well-worn, instantly-recognizable caption-contest joke template or stock phrase nearly verbatim with no new twist (e.g. an 'eat dessert first' line, a 'the remote is in your hand/is plastic' line, a 'do my teeth look big' line, a Hollywood 'what I'd really like to do is direct' line). Score 10 if the premise and phrasing feel genuinely novel rather than a recycled template.
proposals.rationale: R07 'guess i'll go ahead and eat my dessert first' and R11 'in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first' are near-duplicate stock lines; R44 'do you think it makes my teeth look big' and R58 'do my teeth look big in this' are likewise near-duplicates; R28 and R37 both run the same remote-control premise; all are dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Unhedged, direct delivery vs. conversational filler
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption states its content as a clean, direct assertion with no throat-clearing. Score 0 if the caption is opened or padded with conversational hedges/fillers ('i don't know', 'guess i'll', 'actually', 'okay, okay, fine', 'you know') that delay the point.
proposals.rationale: R44 'i don't know. do you think it makes my teeth look big' and R46 'okay, okay. fine, i'll fill out the census' both open with throat-clearing filler before the point; contrast with R01 'no. no quarter will be given', which is unhedged. R44/R46 are dense_low_card_high; R01 is dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Comic timing built from repetition or fragmentation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption uses deliberate word/phrase repetition, staccato fragments, or broken syntax to build comic rhythm or emphasis. Score 0 if the caption is a single smooth, ordinary grammatical sentence with no rhythmic or repetition device.
proposals.rationale: R57 'six feet dude. six. feet' builds its whole effect from fragmented repetition; contrast the smooth single-clause R21 'he got indicted' and R51 'i don't tell you how to gather', which carry no repetition device despite also being terse.

proposals.name: Sustained character voice appropriate to a reimagined role
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption fully commits to and sustains a specific persona or role (e.g. pirate captain, drill sergeant, folk narrator) that recasts the pictured figure, without breaking voice to explain the joke. Score 0 if the caption is delivered in a generic, unmarked contemporary speaking voice with no adopted persona.
proposals.rationale: R01/R14's pirate 'no quarter' phrasing and R48's folksy 'comin' round the mountain' resignation both commit fully to an adopted voice; both pairs are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Multiple comic mechanisms stacked in one short line
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption combines more than one distinct comic device (e.g. a pun plus a register clash, or a literalized idiom plus an implied threat) within a single short line. Score 0 if the caption relies on exactly one simple, single-layer device (one pun, one observation) with nothing else added.
proposals.rationale: R18 'now the house has 88 keys and no locks' stacks a piano-key pun with a security/burglary image; R35's Oxford-comma joke stacks a grammar lesson with an implied cannibalism reading. Both dense_high_card_low; contrast R30 'no, that's a blues jay', a single-layer pun that is dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Caption is keyed to this specific scene, not portable
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption's premise and phrasing clearly depend on and could only belong to one particular pictured scenario. Score 0 if the caption could be dropped into many unrelated cartoons or scenes unchanged and still 'work', i.e. it reads as generic rather than scene-specific.
proposals.rationale: R09 'yes we are your upstairs neighbors- how did you know', R17 'believe it or not, they think that we look alike too', and R32 'you're sure it's wild caught? my in-laws can tell' all read as generic lines that could transplant into many scenes; all three are dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Euphemism or indirection for charged content
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption references something taboo, violent, or embarrassing through euphemism, indirection, or a coy substitution, leaving the reader to do the inferential work rather than stating it outright. Score 0 if charged content is either stated fully explicitly or if the caption contains no charged content to euphemize at all.
proposals.rationale: R48 'she won't be comin' round the mountain' euphemizes death/decline via song reference; R43 'you should see the breasts' uses a double entendre as indirection for a risque reading. Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Joke requires an ironic/sarcastic reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption's literal words must be read as the opposite of, or as ironically undercutting, the sincere sentiment they appear to express, and this reversal carries the entire joke. Score 0 if the caption is sincere and literal throughout, with no ironic inversion required to get the point.
proposals.rationale: R45 'enough about me. you're an accountant? that must be exciting' and R09 'yes we are your upstairs neighbors- how did you know' both depend on reading the surface sentiment as insincere/backhanded; both are dense_low_card_high, testing whether the scorecard over-credits irony detached from a fresher premise.

proposals.name: Oddly precise number anchors the joke
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption includes a specific, unusually precise number or quantity (not a round or generic figure) that intensifies or anchors the comic point. Score 0 if the caption contains no numeric or quantitative detail at all.
proposals.rationale: R24 'given we had 500 this morning' and R60 '581 days without an accident' both use an oddly specific count as the engine of the joke, and both are dense_high_card_low; contrast R52's milder 'it took him six days to make', which is dense_low_card_high, to test whether specificity alone (vs. specificity plus implied dark backstory) drives the dense preference.

proposals.name: Caption brevity / word count
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how short and terse the caption is (word count / clause count), where 10 = an extremely short single clause (roughly <=5 words) and 0 = a long multi-clause caption (roughly >=15 words). Score only the LENGTH of the text; do not judge whether the caption's length helps or hurts it as a joke.
proposals.rationale: Extreme brevity clusters with dense_high_card_low: R15 'he got indicted' (3 words, dense_pct=.957), R56 'wreckmaninoff' (1 word, dense_pct=.794), R25 'you're rambling again' (3 words, dense_pct=.991). Longer, multi-clause captions cluster with dense_low_card_high: R34 (16 words, card_pct=.913), R54 (15 words, card_pct=.824). Length is a production/format habit, not itself contest-worthiness.

proposals.name: Phonetic pun or wordplay density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption's core joke relies on a phonetic pun, near-homophone, or double meaning of a word, where 10 = the entire joke is built on such wordplay and 0 = no wordplay is present. Do not judge whether the pun is clever or funny -- only whether wordplay is present.
proposals.rationale: Puns/wordplay skew heavily dense_high_card_low: R18 'it's so ewe' (dense_pct=.981), R56 'wreckmaninoff' (dense_pct=.794), R24 'i suspect vowel play' (dense_pct=.867). A scorecard built from explicit criteria may not credit phonetic cleverness the way a dense reader's pattern sense does, so mere wordplay presence predicts the disagreement independent of whether the specific pun lands.

proposals.name: Recycled idiom or stock-phrase reuse
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption reuses a common, pre-existing conversational idiom, catchphrase, or cliche scenario applied to this scene, versus an idiosyncratic phrase invented specifically for this scene. 10 = built entirely around a recognizable stock phrase/trope, 0 = entirely original phrasing. Do not judge whether reusing the phrase makes the caption better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Near-duplicate captions recycling the same stock idiom both land dense_low_card_high: the 'no bag' trope (R41 card_pct=.641; R50 card_pct=.991) and the 'teeth look big' trope (R13 card_pct=.979; R46 card_pct=.955). Convergence on a familiar stock line is a hive-mind/bandwagon signature, not evidence of an individual caption's merit.

proposals.name: Real-world political / current-events reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the caption explicitly names or alludes to real-world politics, elections, named political parties/offices, or current-events topics, where 10 = the joke's content is centrally political/current-events and 0 = no such reference at all. Do not judge whether the political reference is appropriate, tasteful, or effective.
proposals.rationale: R39 'republican primary ticket' (dense_pct=.751/card_pct=.042) and R43 'it's the republican slate of candidates' (dense_pct=.764/card_pct=.028) both invoke real-world party politics and both land dense_high_card_low. Whether a caption happens to reference partisan politics is a topic-selection habit, not a measure of how good it is as a caption.

proposals.name: Specific numeric or quantitative detail
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption's joke is built around a specific, concrete number or quantity (a day count, weight, measurement, dollar amount, etc.) stated in the text, where 10 = a specific number is the central device of the joke and 0 = no numbers appear. Do not judge whether the particular number chosen is funny.
proposals.rationale: Specific numeric details recur across dense_high_card_low items: R17 '581 days' (dense_pct=.741), R36 '45 pounds ... a leg' (dense_pct=.656), R49 '88 keys' (dense_pct=.714), R59 '500 this morning' (dense_pct=.880). Reliance on an arbitrary concrete number is a compositional habit that can pattern-match to 'specific = funny' without being the actual source of quality.

proposals.name: Assessment/evaluation vocabulary in the joke
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption's own vocabulary invokes the general idea of being assessed, ranked, evaluated, graded, or reviewed by someone in authority (e.g. a job performance review, a report card, a contest of some kind), in ANY sense, rather than being purely about the depicted physical action in the scene. 10 = assessment/evaluation vocabulary is central to the joke, 0 = no such vocabulary appears anywhere. Do not judge whether this thematic choice is a good comedic device, and do not consider anything about how this particular caption itself fared.
proposals.rationale: R11 'they're still looking for votes' (dense_pct=.970/card_pct=.093) and R29 'all my evaluation said was good girl' (dense_pct=.827/card_pct=.121) both frame the joke around being assessed rather than the depicted action, and both land dense_high_card_low. This resembles a submitter drawing on their own experience navigating a judging/submission apparatus -- an upstream familiarity that would show up as this vocabulary, not as caption quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's repeat-entrant / contest-savvy familiarity with the submission process

proposals.name: Named external media or cultural-property reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the caption explicitly names a specific media franchise, fictional character, celebrity, TV/book property, or branded cultural reference as part of the joke, where 10 = the joke depends entirely on recognizing a specific external cultural reference and 0 = no such reference appears. Do not judge whether the reference is obscure, dated, or well-chosen.
proposals.rationale: R02 (riffing on a named cooking-show catchphrase format, dense_pct=.563/card_pct=.034) and R03 'my dear watson' (a named literary-detective reference, dense_pct=.702/card_pct=.134) both lean on recognizing an external cultural property, and both land dense_high_card_low. This tracks the author's media/cultural literacy rather than the craft of the caption itself.

proposals.name: Scripted policy/customer-service correction register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption is phrased as a scripted policy correction or institutional/customer-service-style statement (e.g. 'actually, it's not X, it's Y', reciting a rule) rather than as a spontaneous personal remark, where 10 = the entire line reads like a rehearsed policy/service script and 0 = it reads like an off-the-cuff personal remark. Do not judge whether this register is funny or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R12 'it's not a grill problem it's a chicken problem' (card_pct=.894), R16 'actually it's no dogs, cats or other small pets' (card_pct=.938), and R20 'you know the remote is plastic, right' (card_pct=.864) all adopt a scripted correction/policy-recitation register and all land dense_low_card_high. A rehearsed institutional-sounding voice is a stylistic habit some submitters bring from day-to-day speech, not a marker of joke quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's professional background in service/policy/administrative roles

proposals.name: Second-person direct address vs third-person narration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the caption directly addresses a 'you' (second-person, speaking straight to another character) rather than describing someone in the third person ('he/she/they') or making a general statement, where 10 = entirely direct second-person address and 0 = entirely third-person/general. Do not judge whether direct address makes the caption land better.
proposals.rationale: Third-person/no-address items cluster dense_high_card_low: R11 'they're still looking for votes' (dense_pct=.970), R15 'he got indicted' (dense_pct=.957). Direct second-person address clusters dense_low_card_high: R04 'honey, the remote is in your hand' (card_pct=.794), R13 'do my teeth look big in this' (card_pct=.979). Grammatical person reflects the submitter's chosen narrative stance, not the caption's merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's assumed relational stance to the depicted subject (intimate address vs distanced narration)

proposals.name: Hedging/qualifying language vs flat declarative delivery
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the caption uses hedging or qualifying language (e.g. 'i don't know', 'i guess', 'i think', 'actually', softening interjections) before its main point, versus stating its point as a flat, confident declarative with no qualifiers, where 10 = heavily hedged/qualified delivery and 0 = a single flat unqualified assertion. Do not judge whether the hedging or the bluntness is the better comedic choice.
proposals.rationale: Hedged, qualifier-laden delivery clusters dense_low_card_high: R30 'enough about me... that must be exciting' (card_pct=.811), R44 'oh, god. i think there's a theme' (card_pct=.890), R19 'i don't know about you, but i'm thinking takeout' (card_pct=.924). Flat unqualified declaratives cluster dense_high_card_low: R10 'you need to get your act together' (dense_pct=.991), R25 'you're rambling again' (dense_pct=.991). This is a register/confidence habit, not itself evidence of quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's conversational register / social confidence in delivery

proposals.name: Compact comic payload
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every word advances a complete setup and payoff with no padding; score 0 when the line is padded, repetitive, or lacks a discernible comic payload.
proposals.rationale: The extreme compression in R07, R45, and R52 suggests value that a checklist may miss when it rewards more explicit construction.

proposals.name: Integrated phonetic pun
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a phonetic or spelling-based pun is unmistakable and meaningfully changes the premise; score 0 when there is no such wordplay or the substitution is arbitrary.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R56 use sound substitutions as the entire comic mechanism, while R51 shows how a simple pun can receive attention without comparable integration.

proposals.name: Idiom literalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom, lyric, or saying is repurposed through a fresh literal or situational reading; score 0 when it is used conventionally with no reinterpretation.
proposals.rationale: R16, R32, and R41 all bend familiar phrases into new situations rather than merely using ordinary wording.

proposals.name: Precision of concrete detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an unusual number, measurement, or physical detail materially sharpens the comic contrast; score 0 when details are absent, vague, or merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: The quantities in R17, R33, and R36 make their reversals unusually vivid and specific.

proposals.name: Clashing interpretive frames
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two incompatible domains or interpretations collide coherently in one line; score 0 when the associations are routine or the juxtaposition is incoherent.
proposals.rationale: R03 collides ornithology with music, R18 combines invasion with soccer practice, and R36 juxtaposes weight loss with amputation.

proposals.name: Deadpan audacity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an absurd, dark, or outrageous premise is delivered in calm matter-of-fact language; score 0 when the line overexplains, emotionally signals, or announces its joke.
proposals.rationale: R09, R17, and R25 state highly charged circumstances with restrained conversational delivery.

proposals.name: Setup-to-turn reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the opening establishes a likely interpretation that a later phrase sharply overturns; score 0 when there is no meaningful turn or the final phrase adds nothing.
proposals.rationale: R01, R47, and R49 each begin conventionally and then redirect the reader through a compact second-beat reversal.

proposals.name: Role or status inversion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line clearly reverses expected roles between people, animals, or authorities; score 0 when every participant behaves in an ordinary role.
proposals.rationale: R22 and R29 invert human-and-animal training roles, while R53 contrasts herding with directing in a similarly role-conscious way.

proposals.name: Distinctive speaker voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when diction reveals a specific persona, attitude, or relationship that could not be voiced neutrally; score 0 when the line could be spoken by anyone without characterization.
proposals.rationale: R28, R42, and R57 convey distinct social attitudes and relationships through voice rather than exposition.

proposals.name: Transformed cultural reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable political, literary, musical, or historical reference is repurposed to create a second comic layer; score 0 when the reference is merely named or used literally.
proposals.rationale: R18, R20, and R58 turn familiar references into active mechanisms instead of decorative allusions.

proposals.name: Punctuation-driven timing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when punctuation, spacing, or repetition creates a materially different reading or comic pause; score 0 when punctuation has no effect beyond ordinary grammar.
proposals.rationale: R43 depends on punctuation to separate radically different readings, while R46 uses repeated fragments and pauses as the central timing device.

proposals.name: Productive reader inference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line withholds exactly enough information for a surprising implication that the reader can readily complete; score 0 when it explains everything or is too underspecified to support a coherent inference.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R24 rely on the reader to complete the semantic connection, rewarding implication rather than explanation.

proposals.name: Non-interchangeable premise
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the premise depends on an unusual combination of circumstances and would not transfer unchanged to many unrelated scenes; score 0 when it is generic banter or a reusable conversational template.
proposals.rationale: The repeated teeth, dessert, and remote formulations in R04, R34, and R59 illustrate interchangeable premises with limited textual identity.

proposals.name: Fresh lexical framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar subject gains a new angle through an unexpected verb, noun, or metaphor; score 0 when the wording is routine even if it is clear and grammatical.
proposals.rationale: Routine phrasing appears in R28, R40, and R60, whereas unusual lexical choices such as collection in R10 or gather in R42 create stronger angles.

proposals.name: Controlled sensitive subject
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when sexual, political, dark, or otherwise sensitive material is specific, restrained, and supported by a clear comic mechanism; score 0 when the line is bland or relies on a provocative word alone.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R20 use sensitive material within constructed premises, while R13 demonstrates why provocation without enough supporting mechanism should score lower.

proposals.name: Telegraphic compression
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much is the caption compressed into an unusually short, fragmentary, or telegraphic form? Judge only visible length and syntax; do not judge whether this is good, funny, or effective.
proposals.rationale: Short, compressed forms appear in R01, R15, R17, and R52, while longer constructions appear in R12 and R39. Compactness can be a detectable style habit without itself indicating caption quality.

proposals.name: Numerical specificity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain explicit numbers, measurements, counts, durations, or clock times? Count only their visible presence; do not judge whether the numerical detail is good or relevant.
proposals.rationale: R06, R18, R20, R51, R53, and R60 contain conspicuous numerical or measurement language. Such specificity is an easily detected subject-matter marker, not a quality assessment.

proposals.name: Taboo body vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use bodily, sexual, anatomical, or socially taboo vocabulary? Score only the extent of such wording; do not judge whether it is amusing, tasteful, or effective.
proposals.rationale: R22 mentions exposed skin and consent, R42 mentions breasts, and R53 contrasts weight loss with a lost leg. Taboo or anatomical vocabulary can attract attention independently of caption quality.

proposals.name: Civic-political topicality
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption invoke elections, political parties, government, public affairs, or political conflict? Judge only the amount of civic-political subject matter; do not judge its insight or humor.
proposals.rationale: Political or civic references occur in R06, R13, R44, R48, and R52. Public-affairs subject matter can trigger familiarity or topical associations without proving anything about the caption's quality.

proposals.name: Pun and homophone density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use puns, homophones, spelling manipulation, or phrase-level wordplay? Count the extent of wordplay only; do not judge whether any wordplay succeeds.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses “ewe,” R04 uses “pull the wool,” R12 exploits punctuation, and R17 uses “wreckmaninoff”; R38 also explicitly mentions vowel play. Wordplay is a surface mechanism that is not identical to quality.

proposals.name: Named cultural allusions
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption rely on recognizable names, cultural references, places, works, genres, or domain-specific allusions? Score only the amount of reference material; do not judge whether the allusion is apt.
proposals.rationale: R17 invokes Rachmaninoff, R24 invokes Saturn, R50 invokes Watson, and R58 invokes a blue jay. Reference density can proxy shared cultural familiarity without being a quality judgement.

proposals.name: Relational dialogue framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption frame a relationship through direct address, kinship, workplace roles, neighbors, or conversational exchange? Judge only visible relational framing; do not judge whether the interaction is funny or believable.
proposals.rationale: R02, R14, R20, R45, R55, and R57 foreground relationships or social roles. An author's intended audience and social network could leave this fingerprint and also shape genuine caption construction, making the channel a sensitivity factor.

proposals.name: Institutional register
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use legal, bureaucratic, organizational, evaluative, or formal public-institution vocabulary? Score only the extent of that register; do not judge whether the wording is sophisticated or effective.
proposals.rationale: R15 uses “indicted,” R22 uses “consent,” R26 uses “evaluation,” and R30, R44, and R52 use civic or organizational language. Professional milieu may produce this textual fingerprint and may also affect underlying writing ability.

proposals.name: Copy-editing residue
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption show visible drafting, copying, or editing residue such as quotation marks, ellipses, dash tails, spacing anomalies, or segmented punctuation? Judge only the artifacts; do not judge whether the text appears polished.
proposals.rationale: R12 contains quotation marks, repeated periods, and a trailing dash; R40 uses unusually segmented punctuation, and R45 contains a spacing anomaly around a hyphen. Editing or transfer workflows could leave these traces and also alter genuine text quality.

proposals.name: Temporal anchoring
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption explicitly anchor itself to time through words such as today, now, this morning, days, duration, sequence, or deadlines? Score only temporal reference; do not judge whether the timing makes the caption effective.
proposals.rationale: R03, R06, R18, R20, R33, and R60 contain explicit temporal anchors. Submission timing can leave topical or deadline-related traces and can also affect how much opportunity the author had to develop the text.

proposals.name: Layered recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption supports two simultaneous readings that sharply reframe each other; score 0 when it has only one straightforward meaning.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R30 turn ordinary wording into a second, consequential interpretation; R57 similarly collides geopolitical and everyday meanings.

proposals.name: Idiomatic literalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom is made literally relevant in a fresh way; score 0 when an idiom is absent or merely repeated conventionally.
proposals.rationale: R07, R09, and R10 exploit the literal meanings of familiar expressions such as coming round, pulling wool, and gathering.

proposals.name: Phonetic word transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike or altered word form creates a clear, sharp comic meaning; score 0 when word sounds or forms do no meaningful work.
proposals.rationale: R15, R46, and R52 derive their central turns from transformed sounds or word forms: wreckmaninoff, ewe, and pooped.

proposals.name: Punctuation-dependent meaning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when punctuation, spacing, or grammatical boundaries materially create the joke; score 0 when the wording works identically without those mechanics.
proposals.rationale: R30 depends on comma placement, while R59 turns the phrase cross word into a semantic and typographic mechanism.

proposals.name: Precision-driven misdirection
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an unusually exact number, time, or detail establishes one expectation and then redirects it; score 0 when specificity is generic or nonfunctional.
proposals.rationale: R11, R28, and R57 use 500, 581 days, and 2:30 as precise anchors for unexpected turns.

proposals.name: Asymmetric comparison
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when parallel wording contrasts mismatched categories or stakes to produce a decisive incongruity; score 0 when no meaningful contrast is present.
proposals.rationale: R39 juxtaposes pounds with a leg, and R54 contrasts piano keys with locks through the same compact structure.

proposals.name: Ethical or social reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption exposes a contradiction, hypocrisy, or power assumption through a concise reversal; score 0 when it offers only a generic opinion.
proposals.rationale: R02 challenges an assumption about consent, while R12 and R19 turn political language into pointed social or institutional commentary.

proposals.name: Cultural allusion repurposing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable cultural, political, literary, or musical reference is substantially reworked for a new comic context; score 0 when it is merely named or quoted.
proposals.rationale: R07 reworks a folk-song phrase, R19 repurposes political terminology, and R59 recasts a Sherlock Holmes-style phrase.

proposals.name: Deadpan escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a flat, matter-of-fact voice treats an increasingly absurd premise as routine; score 0 when the line announces its joke or states absurdity without escalation.
proposals.rationale: R11, R28, and R55 present alarming circumstances in restrained conversational language, letting the escalation carry the humor.

proposals.name: Elliptical inference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when omitted explanation invites one strong, recoverable inference; score 0 when omission makes the caption incoherent or directionless.
proposals.rationale: R10, R34, and R58 leave crucial links unstated while still directing the reader toward a specific implied interpretation.

proposals.name: Punchline compression
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every word contributes setup, turn, or attitude with no filler; score 0 when the line is padded, diffuse, or generic.
proposals.rationale: R42, R48, and R53 achieve their effects through extremely compact wording whose final phrase supplies the entire turn.

proposals.name: Speaker-specific voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the diction reveals a distinctive speaker attitude, status, or personality; score 0 when the line could be spoken by anyone without loss.
proposals.rationale: R27, R42, and R51 characterize speakers through evaluative language, imperious phrasing, and a self-aware accusation of rambling.

proposals.name: Conversational plausibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like a naturally motivated spoken exchange with clear pragmatic intent; score 0 when it sounds forced, contextless, or syntactically unnatural.
proposals.rationale: R04, R06, and R21 are fluent, immediately speakable replies or invitations whose surface dialogue works even apart from a deeper twist.

proposals.name: Direct scene anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption concretely anchors itself in an identifiable object, action, or instruction; score 0 when it remains abstract or could fit almost any situation.
proposals.rationale: R03, R22, and R33 explicitly reference salmon handling, dog commands, and a plastic remote, providing strong literal anchors.

proposals.name: Stock-template independence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption avoids a familiar joke or conversational template while remaining clear; score 0 when it is essentially a standard stock exchange, pun, or reaction.
proposals.rationale: R20, R31, R36, and R45 rely on recurring takeout, dessert-first, or appearance-question formats, making template familiarity a distinct evaluable property.

proposals.name: Current-affairs topic cues
proposals.instruction: How much explicit political, governmental, or current-affairs vocabulary is present? Score only the extent of this topic cue; do not judge whether it is good, funny, or effective.
proposals.rationale: Topic markers may trigger topical familiarity or reader priors independently of caption construction. Examples include R01, R13, R27, R35, and R59.

proposals.name: Taboo/body vocabulary
proposals.instruction: How much sexual, bodily, consent-related, or otherwise taboo vocabulary is present? Score only the amount of this subject matter; do not judge whether it improves the caption.
proposals.rationale: Sensitive subject matter can prompt reactions or filtering unrelated to entry quality. The pattern appears in R10, R14, R31, and R43.

proposals.name: Phonetic wordplay
proposals.instruction: How much phonetic, homophonic, spelling-based, or sound-based wordplay is present? Score only its extent; do not judge whether the wordplay is good or funny.
proposals.rationale: A visible concentration of sound manipulation may attract model or reader heuristics independently of overall caption quality. Examples include R03, R18, R32, and R42.

proposals.name: Borrowed idiom templates
proposals.instruction: How much of the text reuses a familiar idiom, slogan, song phrase, quotation, or recognizable cultural template? Score only the degree of reuse; do not judge whether the reference is effective.
proposals.rationale: Familiar phrasing can supply recognition or cultural-prior effects without indicating intrinsic contest quality. Examples include R09, R12, R21, R25, R39, and R50.

proposals.name: Numerical specificity
proposals.instruction: How much explicit numerical, measured, counted, dated, or quantified detail is present? Score only the amount of quantification; do not judge whether the detail is useful or clever.
proposals.rationale: Numbers can trigger specificity heuristics or rubric reactions unrelated to the caption's underlying quality. Examples include R16, R23, R36, R38, R43, and R45.

proposals.name: Informal typography
proposals.instruction: How much lowercase styling, contractions, unconventional punctuation, ellipses, dashes, spacing, or other informal typography is present? Score only the visible extent; do not judge whether the presentation is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Orthographic style may proxy platform conventions or author habits rather than contest quality. Examples include R06, R17, R29, and R45.

proposals.name: Contest-register dialogue
proposals.instruction: How much the caption uses a familiar spoken-exchange format, including direct address, conversational hedges, or question-and-answer setup? Score only the extent of this register; do not judge whether the dialogue is effective.
proposals.rationale: Familiarity with the caption venue may leave a conventional conversational fingerprint, which can influence processing independently of quality; that familiarity could also help genuine craft. Examples include R04, R07, R11, R26, R30, and R60.

proposals.name: Time-sensitive anchoring
proposals.instruction: How much the text contains explicit present-moment, date-sensitive, event-sensitive, or rapidly time-bound references? Score only the extent of temporal anchoring; do not judge whether topicality is good.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can leave transient references that affect contextual salience independently of wording quality, while topical timing may also contribute to genuine entry quality. Examples include R16, R23, R27, R35, R38, and R54.

proposals.name: Copyedited presentation
proposals.instruction: How much the text displays visible formalization or copyediting markers, such as standardized punctuation, capitalization, balanced syntax, or carefully delimited clauses? Score only the extent of those markers; do not judge correctness or quality.
proposals.rationale: Professional assistance can produce a recognizable presentation style that biases text-based assessment, and the same assistance may genuinely improve the entry. Examples include R06, R21, R29, and R43.

proposals.name: Status and role cues
proposals.instruction: How much the text contains explicit occupational, hierarchical, credential, authority, or institutional-role language? Score only the amount of such language; do not judge whether the status cue makes the caption better.
proposals.rationale: Author background may leave status-related lexical traces that attract assumptions independently of caption quality, while experience or networks could also support genuinely better work. Examples include R19, R33, R37, and R55.
